data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":{"adopted_commitment_refs":[],"disanalogies":["Polanyi's framing concerns whether tacit knowledge can be articulated at all; here the checklist is given and the question is empirical reliability, not philosophical commensurability.","Here we can measure outcomes objectively, so the dispute is resolvable by data rather than by conceptual analysis.","The panel adds an aggregation layer not present in the standard tacit-knowledge framing."],"overturn_conditions":["If panelists using the checklist are shown to match expert performance specifically on atypical, configural cases, the tacit-knowledge bottleneck is empirically refuted for this task.","If the checklist is shown to encode configural rules (e.g., 'If feature A is present and feature B is absent, escalate'), it has articulated the tacit knowledge, contradicting the claim that it cannot be encoded."],"shared_structure":["A mechanistic procedure (checklist) is compared to a holistic process (intuition) for a task where the outcome is objectively scorable.","The question is whether the mechanistic procedure captures the information content of the holistic process.","Tacit knowledge that is not articulated poses a challenge to the mechanistic procedure's completeness."],"source_memory_refs":["SRC_001","SRC_002"],"transfer_claims":["As in the tacit-knowledge argument, the checklist's reliability on surface features may mask an inability to handle the deep features that determine outcomes in edge cases.","The evidence that would distinguish genuine expertise from mere checklist compliance is the same: performance on novel, atypical cases where surface and deep features diverge."]},"claim":"The non-expert panel will NOT be more reliable than the expert for objectively verifiable tasks, because checklists cannot encode the tacit feature-detection that makes expert intuition accurate; the panel's checklist-compliance merely mimics expertise on easy cases and collapses on the hard cases that determine overall reliability.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the task is genuinely decomposable into independent features with no configural interactions (e.g., 'Does the document contain a date in field 3?'), the checklist will match or beat the expert, and the panel's aggregation will reduce noise.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the expert is poorly calibrated due to overconfidence or affective bias, the panel's mechanical procedure may outperform even on configural tasks.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the checklist is adaptive\u2014branching based on earlier answers in a way that captures configural dependencies\u2014the tacit-knowledge objection is weakened.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Expert intuition, in domains with verifiable outcomes, is typically the product of deliberate practice generating rapid pattern matching to diagnostic constellations. A checklist decomposes the judgment into isolated features, but the diagnostic value of a feature often depends on its context (configural processing). Non-experts applying the checklist item-by-item lose configural information. Therefore the panel's apparent reliability on items the checklist happens to cover is not a genuine competence transfer; it is a local heuristic that fails when features appear in atypical configurations\u2014which are precisely the cases where expert intuition excels.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
